passages.t: ‘God presides in the divine assembly’: the judges judged
passages.happening:
This short psalm is set in a courtroom. The heading reads, “A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). Then: “God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods” (verse 1).

God speaks first, and he speaks as a judge charging other judges. “How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?” (verse 2). He tells them what they should have done. “Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed” (verse 3). “Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked” (verse 4).

But they have not done it. “They do not know or understand; they wander in the darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken” (verse 5). When those who judge go wrong, the whole world starts to shake.
passages.hearers:
People in the ancient world often pictured heaven as a royal court. In texts found at Ugarit, the chief god sits over an assembly of gods. The Bible also speaks of beings around God's throne. The prophet Micaiah saw “the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him” (1 Kings 22:19). In Job, “the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD” (Job 1:6).

So a first hearer would picture a great council. But in this psalm, the God of Israel is not one member among many. He stands up in the middle of it and puts the others on trial.

Notice what the charge is. It is not a crime of worship. It is a crime of justice. The weak, the orphan, the poor have been left without anyone to defend them. In Israel those were the people God most often told his judges to protect. The prophets made the same charge against Israel's own leaders.
passages.later:
Isaiah spoke against rulers who “do not defend the fatherless, and the plea of the widow never comes before them” (Isaiah 1:23). James wrote, “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).

Jesus began his work by reading from Isaiah that he had come “to preach good news to the poor” and “to release the oppressed” (Luke 4:18).
passages.asks:
Psalm 82 says that God judges the judges. Anyone with power over others, a parent, a boss, a teacher, a pastor, a judge, will answer to him for how the weak were treated.

Who in your world is weak and has no one to speak for them? This psalm says that defending them is not a hobby for a few. It is what God expects of everyone given any kind of power.

passages.t: ‘You are gods’, ‘But like mortals you will die’
passages.happening:
Then God passes sentence. “I have said, ‘You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.’ But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall” (verses 6 to 7). Whatever their high rank, they will fall like any human ruler.

Then the psalmist speaks for himself, and turns from the failed judges to the true one. “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance” (verse 8).
passages.hearers: The Hebrew word for ‘gods’ here is elohim. It is the usual word for God, but it can also mean other mighty beings, and in a few places it seems to be used of human judges. In Exodus a servant is brought “before the judges” (Exodus 21:6), and there the Hebrew word is elohim.
passages.later: Jesus quoted this verse. When he was accused of blasphemy for calling himself God's Son, he replied, “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’?” (John 10:34). He went on to say that Scripture called them gods ‘to whom the word of God came’, and that Scripture cannot be broken. Then what of the one the Father set apart and sent into the world (John 10:35-36)? His point runs from smaller to greater. If Scripture could call them ‘gods’, he cannot be guilty of blasphemy for calling himself the Son of God.
passages.hard:
Who are the ‘gods’ of verse 6? The book page lists this among the hardest passages in the Psalms. Readers have given three main answers, and each is held by careful people.

Some read them as human rulers and judges. They judged in God's name, so they were given a high title. Their sins, unfair rulings and neglect of the poor, are the sins of human courts. And Jesus speaks of those “to whom the word of God came” (John 10:35), which many take to mean people.

Others read them as heavenly beings, members of God's council who were given charge over the nations and ruled them badly. They point to the setting in verse 1, to the scenes in 1 Kings 22 and Job 1, and to verse 7. To say ‘you will die like mortals’ is only surprising, they say, if the ones addressed are not mortals.

An old Jewish reading, found in the Talmud, takes the words as spoken to Israel at Mount Sinai. Given God's word, they might have been free of death, but they lost that through sin.

None of these readings means that there are other gods equal to the LORD. On every reading, those called ‘gods’ answer to him and will fall. These notes do not choose between them, and each can make sense of Jesus' words in John 10.
passages.asks:
Verse 8 is a prayer you can pray when the courts and the powerful fail: ‘Arise, O God, judge the earth.’ It does not give up on justice. It hands it to the one judge who will not fail.

And let verse 7 humble anyone with power. However high the title, everyone dies, and everyone answers to God.
